regenerable_on: any systemd guest with a journal and python3, staged as harness/bin/se-capture-guest's logs case expects — it stages src/ to /tmp/secmp/src itself now, and binds the adapters package in sys.modules before importing so that ONE adapter loads rather than all twenty with their third-party dependencies. The capture must be PRIVILEGED: an unprivileged journalctl sees only the invoking user's own entries, which is a specimen of a session rather than of a machine. The exact 100 entries are whatever the guest had been doing, so a re-stage re-reads the anchors by hand in the same change — what must be reproduced is the SHAPES, not the sentences: at least one entry carrying a MESSAGE_ID and one carrying none, and at least two distinct priorities.
anonymisation_note:
Through BOTH halves of the gate, and this is the variant that could not exist until two rulings landed on 2026-08-19 — it is the first journal capture this corpus has ever held.

135 substitutions: boot ids, machine ids, invocation ids, stream ids, cursors, the hostname, and the usernames written inside log sentences. Every 32-hex identity carries the 5cb0 scrub marker afterwards, which is how the independent detectors tell a substituted one from a real one.

Two values do NOT follow that pattern, and each was a queue item that blocked this capture outright.

MESSAGE_ID is preserved VERBATIM and must be. It is 32 hex — the machine-id shape — but it is systemd's catalogue id for a message TYPE, compiled into the software and byte-identical on every machine. Substituting it destroys the join to systemd's own catalogue; classifying the FIELD as harmless would disarm the machine-id detector for every payload. Neither was acceptable, and §21 forbids the repair from being on the manifest side at all, because a checker told what the collector believes shares the collector's blind spots. So the detectors now carry systemd's published catalogue as a VALUE allowlist — 99 ids, regenerable with `journalctl --list-catalog`, restated exactly as REPLAY_BOOT_ID and NIL_UUID already are. All 9 distinct MESSAGE_IDs in this capture are in it. A 32-hex value in that field that is NOT a catalogue constant is still a finding, so nothing was weakened: USER_INVOCATION_ID, which lives beside it and is a real identity, is substituted and would be caught if it were not.

The SSH key fingerprint is the other, and it is the one neither gate caught. `Accepted publickey … ED25519 SHA256:<43 base64 chars>` survived the scrubber AND the detectors verbatim in the first attempt at this capture: `prose` substitutes shapes and --hostnames removes chosen words, and a base64 hash is neither. A green --check on that payload was a FALSE CLEAN, which is the precise failure this gate exists to prevent. Both halves now know the shape — separately, and deliberately not from a shared regex — so the scrubber replaces it with a fingerprint of the same rendering carrying this tool's ANON marker, and the checker passes a marked one and still flags an unmarked one, including one whose body merely contains ANON somewhere other than the start.
note:
The journal is the one interface here that is UNBOUNDED, and every property of this variant follows from that.

logs has no acquire(). That is the design rather than an omission: a bounded query has no 'all items' to hand over, so the adapter's only materialising verb is collect(), and the replay seam declares the page it drives beside the collector instead of inferring it. The page is the plainest the contract admits — no filters, no cursor, limit=None so the bound is the adapter's own DEFAULT_LIMIT rather than a number the harness chose.

A row is one journal entry, named by its __CURSOR, and the cursor is scrubbed like any other identity — it embeds the boot id and the sequence number. So the object names in this pair are substituted values, and a re-stage produces different ones.

Two facts on every row come from the PAGE and not from the entry: RepeatCount and RepeatWindow. A single entry has no window to count within, so get_object cannot produce them and the two surfaces legitimately differ — SPEC rule 14 permits that and requires it documented, which is what the adapter's own comment does. They are the only facts in this product whose value depends on which other rows were asked for.

Stated bounds.

The capture observes its own capture. Entries near the head are `sudo python3 -c ...` running the instrumented acquisition, and its _CMDLINE is the capture script itself. That is honest — it is what the machine was doing — but a reader should not mistake it for a specimen of ordinary activity.

Every entry here is priority 5 or 6. No error, no critical, no emerg, so the whole severity ladder in rules/logs.py above `notice` is evaluated by nothing in this pair, and the opinions it can form are unexercised.

All 100 entries fit one page, so the pagination this collection exists to bound is never actually bounded: no cursor is issued, no truncation happens, and MAX_LIMIT is not approached.

No entry carries a CONTAINER_NAME, so the container join is unvisited — this guest ran no containers at capture time.
anchors_note:
Read off payloads/r---n--100.json by hand at staging, before any stream existed.

The object is named by the entry's __CURSOR because that is the row's NATIVE name — the id the adapter mints is `entry:<cursor>`, and the collator derives it from the declared prefix and this name, so an anchor on the id would assert the collator's work rather than the collector's. The cursors are the SCRUBBED ones, which is the only form this committed pair contains.

Priority 6 is anchored as an INTEGER and that is the point of it. The journal answers `"PRIORITY": "6"` — a STRING — and the adapter converts it, because a severity that sorts lexically puts 10 before 2. A port that passed the member through emits `"Priority": "6"`, which satisfies no typed comparison, and typed equality catches that where an eyeball reading `6` would not.

Timestamp is anchored because it is the other real derivation on the row: `__REALTIME_TIMESTAMP` is microseconds since the epoch as a decimal STRING, and the fact is an ISO instant. 1787151273220377 -> 2026-08-19T14:54:33Z, computed with the adapter's own usec_to_iso against the captured number rather than copied out of a stream. A port that divided by the wrong power of ten lands in 1970 or in the far future, and both are obvious against this value and invisible against a relative one.

MessageId present on one row and ABSENT on another is the pair that matters most in this variant, for a reason beyond the collector: it is what makes the catalogue-allowlist ruling checkable from the corpus side. The value anchored is a real systemd catalogue id, preserved through the scrub because it names a message type rather than a machine, and the absence beside it proves the fact is emitted from the entry rather than defaulted — a port that minted a MessageId for every row satisfies the first anchor and fails the second.

SyslogIdentifier is anchored on both rows, with different values, because it is the cheapest way to prove the two anchors are addressing two DIFFERENT entries. Two cursors that differ only in a sequence number are easy to transpose while reading, and `systemd` beside `sudo` makes a transposition fail loudly.

commit_objects 100 is anchored because absence is not the only way to lose a collection. The page is driven with limit=None so the bound is the adapter's DEFAULT_LIMIT; a port that hardcoded a different default, or that applied MAX_LIMIT instead, emits a different count from the identical payload and satisfies every fact anchor above.

Deliberately NOT anchored: RepeatCount and RepeatWindow. Both are on every row and both are PAGE-scoped — their values depend on which other entries were asked for, so anchoring one would pin a property of this harness's page rather than of the machine. The bound is stated in the note instead. `_BOOT_ID`, `_MACHINE_ID`, `_CMDLINE`, `_EXE` and the rest of the trusted-field block are in the payload and reach no row at all, because a fact must be cited by an opinion, used in identity or a relation, or be part of the declared answer (DESIGN 15).
